warmup.q: A worker is inside Thread.sleep(10_000). Another thread calls worker.interrupt(). The worker catches the InterruptedException. Inside the catch block, what does Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() return?
options: true, because it was just interrupted
false, because the flag was cleared when the exception was thrown
warmup.why: Methods that throw InterruptedException clear the interrupt flag first. So inside the catch the flag is already false. If the catch block only logs, the stop request is lost for good. That is why the rule is to restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(), or rethrow.

sections.h: A thread is always in one of six states
sections.html:
Call t.getState() and you get one of six values of the Thread.State enum. Thread dumps print the same names, so learning them now pays off every time you debug a stuck service.

State What the thread is doing
NEW Created, but start() has not been called.
RUNNABLE Running, or ready to run and waiting for a core.
BLOCKED Waiting to enter a synchronized block that another thread holds.
WAITING Waiting with no time limit: Object.wait(), join(), LockSupport.park().
TIMED_WAITING The same with a time limit: sleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms).
TERMINATED run() has returned or thrown.

Three of these surprise people.

RUNNABLE does not mean "using a CPU". The Javadoc says the thread is executing in the JVM "but it may be waiting for other resources from the operating system such as processor." A thread waiting its turn for a core is RUNNABLE. So is a thread stuck in a socket read from Oracle, because the JVM only sees that it is inside native code. A thread dump full of RUNNABLE threads can still be a service that does nothing.

BLOCKED is only for synchronized. A thread waiting for a ReentrantLock (lesson 7 of this track) is parked, so it shows WAITING. If you search a dump for BLOCKED to find lock contention, you'll miss every explicit lock.

TERMINATED is final. A thread cannot be restarted. If you need the work done again, you create a new thread, or better, hand the task to a pool.

try.title: Put a thread in every state
steps: Read ThreadStates below. For each show(...) line, predict the state before you run it.
Run it with the command below.
Find the line the waiter prints when it is interrupted out of wait(). Keep it in mind for the third section.

code.title: ThreadStates.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** Puts threads into each of the six states and prints what getState() reports. */ public class ThreadStates { static final Object monitor = new Object(); static volatile boolean spin = true; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread sleeper = new Thread(() -> pause(2_000), "sleeper"); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", "before start():", sleeper.getState()); sleeper.start(); show(sleeper, Thread.State.TIMED_WAITING, "inside sleep(2000):"); Thread busy = new Thread(() -> { while (spin) Thread.onSpinWait(); }, "busy"); busy.start(); show(busy, Thread.State.RUNNABLE, "in a busy loop:"); Thread waiter = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (monitor) { try { monitor.wait(); // no timeout } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("waiter interrupted, flag now " + Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()); } } }, "waiter"); waiter.start(); show(waiter, Thread.State.WAITING, "inside wait():"); Thread blocked = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (monitor) { } }, "blocked"); synchronized (monitor) { // main holds the monitor... blocked.start(); // ...so this thread cannot enter show(blocked, Thread.State.BLOCKED, "entering a held lock:"); } spin = false; waiter.interrupt(); for (Thread t : new Thread[] {sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked}) t.interrupt(); for (Thread t : new Thread[] {sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked}) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", "after join():", sleeper.getState()); } // getState() is a snapshot, so poll until the thread gets where we sent it static void show(Thread t, Thread.State expected, String label) throws InterruptedException { for (int i = 0; i < 200 && t.getState() != expected; i++) Thread.sleep(10); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", label, t.getState()); } static void pause(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: ThreadStates.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Puts threads into each of the six states and prints what getState() reports. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val monitor = Object() // java.lang.Object, because Kotlin's Any has no wait() @Volatile private var spin = true fun main() { val sleeper = Thread({ pause(2_000) }, "sleeper") println("%-24s%s".format("before start():", sleeper.state)) sleeper.start() show(sleeper, Thread.State.TIMED_WAITING, "inside sleep(2000):") val busy = thread(name = "busy") { while (spin) Thread.onSpinWait() } show(busy, Thread.State.RUNNABLE, "in a busy loop:") val waiter = thread(name = "waiter") { synchronized(monitor) { try { monitor.wait() // no timeout } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("waiter interrupted, flag now ${Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted}") } } } show(waiter, Thread.State.WAITING, "inside wait():") val blocked = Thread({ synchronized(monitor) { } }, "blocked") synchronized(monitor) { // main holds the monitor... blocked.start() // ...so this thread cannot enter show(blocked, Thread.State.BLOCKED, "entering a held lock:") } spin = false val all = listOf(sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked) all.forEach { it.interrupt() } all.forEach { it.join() } println("%-24s%s".format("after join():", sleeper.state)) } // getState() is a snapshot, so poll until the thread gets where we sent it private fun show(t: Thread, expected: Thread.State, label: String) { var i = 0 while (i++ < 200 && t.state != expected) Thread.sleep(10) println("%-24s%s".format(label, t.state)) } private fun pause(ms: Long) { try { Thread.sleep(ms) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } }

try.expect: You'll see NEW, TIMED_WAITING (in sleep), RUNNABLE (busy loop), WAITING (in wait()), BLOCKED (main holds the monitor) and finally TERMINATED. The waiter prints flag now false: the interrupt woke it, and the flag was cleared on the way out.

sections.h: Wait with join(), because sleep() only passes time
sections.html:
join() is how one thread waits for another to finish. It comes in three forms:

Java
t.join();                                          // wait as long as it takes
t.join(500);                                       // wait up to 500 ms, then return either way
boolean ended = t.join(Duration.ofMillis(500));    // JDK 19+: says whether it ended
Kotlin
t.join()                                           // wait as long as it takes
t.join(500)                                        // wait up to 500 ms, then return either way
val ended = t.join(Duration.ofMillis(500))         // JDK 19+: says whether it ended

After a timed join, check t.isAlive() (or the boolean) to learn whether the thread ended or you simply stopped waiting.

join() does a second job, and it matters more than the waiting. When join() returns, the calling thread is guaranteed to see everything the finished thread wrote. The java.util.concurrent docs put it this way: "All actions in a thread happen-before any other thread successfully returns from a join on that thread." That is why the lab in lesson 1 of this track (Threads from zero) could read the partial array after the joins with no locks at all.

Thread.sleep(ms) gives you neither. It pauses the current thread for at least that long and promises nothing about any other thread. This code is a race:

Java
worker.start();
Thread.sleep(100);          // "should be enough"
use(worker.result);         // may still be unset
Kotlin
worker.start()
Thread.sleep(100)           // "should be enough"
use(worker.result)          // may still be unset

On a quiet laptop the worker finishes in 2 ms and the code works. On a loaded CI agent, or a pod sharing its node with a batch job, it doesn't. And even when the worker has finished, the language gives sleep no synchronization meaning, so main is not promised to see result. Replace the sleep with join() and both problems go away.

Use sleep for what it is: a pause. A back-off between retries to the card issuer, or a poll interval. Since JDK 19 you can write Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(200)) if you like the unit in the type.

try.title: Give up waiting, then wait properly
steps: Read JoinWithTimeout. The worker takes about 500 ms. Predict both printed lines.
Change the timed join to fetch.join(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) and run again. What does ended say now, and how long did main wait?

code.title: JoinWithTimeout.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; import java.time.Duration; /** join(timeout) gives up waiting; join() waits for the end and makes the result visible. */ public class JoinWithTimeout { static long rateCents; // plain field: join() is what makes the write visible public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread fetch = new Thread(() -> { sleepQuietly(500); // stands in for a 500 ms call to an FX-rate service rateCents = 10_842; }, "fx-fetch"); fetch.start(); boolean ended = fetch.join(Duration.ofMillis(100)); // JDK 19+: returns whether it ended System.out.println("after join(100 ms): ended=" + ended + ", alive=" + fetch.isAlive() + ", rate=" + rateCents); fetch.join(); // no timeout: wait for the end System.out.println("after join(): alive=" + fetch.isAlive() + ", rate=" + rateCents); } static void sleepQuietly(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: JoinWithTimeout.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import java.time.Duration import kotlin.concurrent.thread // join(timeout) gives up waiting; join() waits for the end and makes the result visible. private var rateCents = 0L // plain field: join() is what makes the write visible fun main() { val fetch = thread(name = "fx-fetch") { try { Thread.sleep(500) // stands in for a 500 ms call to an FX-rate service } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } rateCents = 10_842 } val ended = fetch.join(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // JDK 19+: returns whether it ended println("after join(100 ms): ended=$ended, alive=${fetch.isAlive}, rate=$rateCents") fetch.join() // no timeout: wait for the end println("after join(): alive=${fetch.isAlive}, rate=$rateCents") }

try.expect: First run: ended=false, alive=true, rate=0, then alive=false, rate=10842. With a 2-second limit, ended=true and the rate is already there after about 500 ms: a timed join returns as soon as the thread ends, it does not wait out the full time.

sections.h: Interrupt is a polite request, and the flag is easy to lose
sections.html:
Java has no safe way to kill a thread. It has interrupt(), which asks. t.interrupt() sets a flag on t, and what happens next depends on what t is doing:

  • If it is blocked in sleep, wait or join, or in a blocking call such as BlockingQueue.take(), that call throws InterruptedException.
  • Otherwise nothing happens right away. The flag stays set until the thread looks at it.

The thread looks with Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted(), which only reads the flag, or with the static Thread.interrupted(), which reads it and clears it. Use the first one unless you really mean to consume the request.

Now the detail behind most interrupt bugs. Methods that throw InterruptedException clear the flag before they throw. So inside your catch block the flag is already false. If you log the exception and carry on, the request is gone. The loop around you never learns it was asked to stop, and executor.shutdownNow(), which works by interrupting, can't stop your task.

The rule has two options. Let the exception propagate (declare throws InterruptedException), or restore the flag before you do anything else:

Java
try {
    Thread.sleep(backoffMillis);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // put the request back
    return;                               // then stop, or throw your own exception
}
Kotlin
try {
    Thread.sleep(backoffMillis)           // Kotlin compiles this without a try, so add one on purpose
} catch (e: InterruptedException) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt()    // put the request back
    return                                // then stop, or throw your own exception
}

The JDK's own engineers get this wrong too. JDK 23 fixed ImageIcon.loadImage to restore the flag, and JDK 24 fixed the same bug in FileSystemPreferences.lockFile(). From JDK 26 the Thread Javadoc has a section on interruption that states the rule above in so many words.

One more case. A loop that never blocks, such as one that publishes batch after batch while the outbox is full, never meets an InterruptedException. It must check isInterrupted() itself, once per iteration or once per batch. Otherwise the interrupt cannot reach it.

try.title: Watch the flag disappear
steps: Run InterruptFlag and read the five numbered lines.
Comment out the line me.interrupt() in the catch block. Predict lines 2 to 5, then run again.
Explain to yourself why line 4 prints true the first time and why line 5 then prints false.

code.title: InterruptFlag.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** Watch the interrupt flag: set by interrupt(), cleared when sleep() throws, restored by you. */ public class InterruptFlag { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { Thread me = Thread.currentThread(); try { Thread.sleep(10_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("1. caught InterruptedException, flag is now " + me.isInterrupted()); me.interrupt(); // restore it: comment this line out and run again System.out.println("2. after interrupt(), flag is " + me.isInterrupted()); } System.out.println("3. isInterrupted() only reads it: " + me.isInterrupted()); System.out.println("4. Thread.interrupted() reads AND clears: " + Thread.interrupted()); System.out.println("5. so now the flag is " + me.isInterrupted()); }, "worker"); worker.start(); Thread.sleep(200); worker.interrupt(); // a request, not a command worker.join(); } }

alt.title: InterruptFlag.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Watch the interrupt flag: set by interrupt(), cleared when sleep() throws, restored by you. fun main() { val worker = thread(name = "worker") { val me = Thread.currentThread() try { Thread.sleep(10_000) // Kotlin doesn't force this try/catch on you } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("1. caught InterruptedException, flag is now ${me.isInterrupted}") me.interrupt() // restore it: comment this line out and run again println("2. after interrupt(), flag is ${me.isInterrupted}") } println("3. isInterrupted only reads it: ${me.isInterrupted}") println("4. Thread.interrupted() reads AND clears: ${Thread.interrupted()}") println("5. so now the flag is ${me.isInterrupted}") } Thread.sleep(200) worker.interrupt() // a request, not a command worker.join() }

try.expect: With the restore: false, true, true, true, false. Line 1 is false because sleep cleared the flag. Line 4 consumes it, so line 5 is false. Without the restore, every line after the first prints false: the request was lost the moment the exception was caught.

sections.h: Daemon threads, and the stop button Java took away
sections.html:
A daemon thread is one the JVM will not wait for. When the last non-daemon thread ends, the JVM exits and any daemon threads stop wherever they are. Their finally blocks do not run.

Java
Thread flusher = new Thread(this::flushMetrics, "metrics-flusher");
flusher.setDaemon(true);   // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException
flusher.start();
Kotlin
val flusher = Thread(this::flushMetrics, "metrics-flusher")
flusher.isDaemon = true    // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException
flusher.start()            // or in one go: thread(name = "metrics-flusher", isDaemon = true) { flushMetrics() }

A new thread copies the daemon setting of the thread that created it, so threads started from main are non-daemon. The JVM's own helpers, like Finalizer and Signal Dispatcher from lesson 1 of this track, are daemons. Daemon threads suit background work you can afford to lose halfway: a cache refresher, a metrics flusher. They are the wrong choice for anything that writes to the ledger or commits a Kafka offset, because the JVM can cut them off between the write and the commit.

So how do you stop a thread that would not finish on its own? You interrupt it, and it stops itself. Java once had a real stop button. Thread.stop() threw an error inside the target thread wherever it happened to be, which released its locks and left half-updated objects for other threads to find. It was deprecated in Java 1.2, made to always throw UnsupportedOperationException in JDK 20, and removed in JDK 26. suspend() and resume() were removed in JDK 23. Old code that still calls stop() fails with NoSuchMethodError on JDK 26 and later.

That leaves cooperative cancellation as the only kind there is: interrupt asks, the thread checks, cleans up and returns. Every executor, framework and pool you use is built on that contract. A task that swallows an interrupt doesn't just ignore one request. It breaks shutdown for every layer above it.

try.title: Lose a finally block
steps: Run DaemonDemo. Count the flushes and look for the finally line.
Change setDaemon(true) to setDaemon(false) (in Kotlin, isDaemon = true to false) and run it again. Stop it with Ctrl+C when you have seen enough.
Keep it non-daemon, and add metrics.interrupt(); metrics.join(); just before main's last println. Run it once more.

code.title: DaemonDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive. Its finally block does not run either. */ public class DaemonDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread metrics = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int i = 1; ; i++) { System.out.println("metrics: flush " + i); Thread.sleep(200); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { System.out.println("metrics: finally block ran"); } }, "metrics-flusher"); metrics.setDaemon(true); // must be called before start(); try false metrics.start(); Thread.sleep(700); System.out.println("main: done, returning"); } }

alt.title: DaemonDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 // A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive. Its finally block does not run either. fun main() { val metrics = Thread({ try { var i = 1 while (true) { println("metrics: flush ${i++}") Thread.sleep(200) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } finally { println("metrics: finally block ran") } }, "metrics-flusher") metrics.isDaemon = true // must be set before start(); try false metrics.start() // (or: thread(isDaemon = true) { ... }) Thread.sleep(700) println("main: done, returning") }

try.expect: As a daemon: four flushes, main: done, returning, and no finally block ran. The JVM exited under it. As a non-daemon it flushes forever, because nothing asks it to stop. With the interrupt and join, it stops at once and prints finally block ran before main finishes. That is a clean shutdown.

analogy: Interrupting a thread is like putting a sticky note on a colleague's monitor that says "please wrap up". If they are asleep at their desk (in sleep or wait), the note wakes them. If they are busy typing, they see it only when they look up, so a good colleague looks up between tasks. The trap is that waking up removes the note: if they read it, shrug and go back to sleep, nobody knows the request was ever made. Restoring the flag means sticking the note back on the monitor for whoever comes next. The analogy breaks because a colleague can ask what you wanted. A thread that clears the flag has no way to recover the request.
world: Every shutdown in your stack is an interrupt in the end. When Quarkus stops, or Kubernetes sends SIGTERM during a rollout, executors call shutdownNow(), which interrupts their worker threads. A Kafka consumer loop that catches InterruptedException around a sleep back-off and carries on will keep the pod alive until the grace period runs out and the kubelet kills it, possibly halfway through a batch of offset commits. A Temporal activity that retries a card-issuer call with Thread.sleep between attempts has the same problem. Search your code for catch (InterruptedException and check each one either rethrows or calls Thread.currentThread().interrupt().
mistake: The most common real mistake is the empty or log-only catch: catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted", e); } inside a loop. People write it because Java forces them to catch the checked exception and the quickest way to make the compiler happy is to log it. Because the flag is cleared when the exception is thrown, the stop request vanishes and the loop runs on. The fix is one line, Thread.currentThread().interrupt();, followed by leaving the loop, or declaring throws InterruptedException and letting it propagate.

compare.title: An interruptible polling loop in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: Thread relay = new Thread(() -> { Thread me = Thread.currentThread(); while (!me.isInterrupted()) { // poll the outbox and publish here try { Thread.sleep(50); // the compiler forces you to handle the checked exception } catch (InterruptedException e) { me.interrupt(); // restore the flag, so the loop condition sees it } } System.out.println("relay stopped, flag = " + me.isInterrupted()); }, "outbox-relay"); relay.start();

kotlin.title: KotlinRelay.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A polling loop that follows the interruption protocol, in Kotlin. fun main() { val relay = thread(name = "outbox-relay") { val me = Thread.currentThread() while (!me.isInterrupted) { // property syntax for isInterrupted() // poll the outbox and publish here try { Thread.sleep(50) // no try/catch is forced on you in Kotlin... } catch (e: InterruptedException) { me.interrupt() // ...but the protocol is the same: restore the flag } } println("relay stopped, flag = ${me.isInterrupted}") } Thread.sleep(300) relay.interrupt() relay.join() println("relay alive after join: ${relay.isAlive}") }

compare.note: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so Thread.sleep(50) compiles without any try/catch. That changes the failure mode. In Java the usual bug is an empty catch that swallows the interrupt. In Kotlin the usual bug is no catch at all: the InterruptedException escapes the lambda, the thread dies with a stack trace on standard error, and any cleanup after the loop never runs. Neither is a clean stop. The protocol is the same in both languages: catch it where you can do something sensible, restore the flag, and leave. isInterrupted reads as a property in Kotlin, and the static Thread.interrupted() still clears the flag.

worked.title: Make a retrying card-issuer call cancellable

steps.say: This retry loop calls the card issuer and backs off on timeouts. Read it and find where a shutdown request disappears.
steps.code: AuthResult authorize(AuthRequest req) { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return issuer.authorize(req); } catch (IssuerTimeoutException e) { try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { log.warn("interrupted during back-off", ie); // and loop again } } } }

alt.html: fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): AuthResult { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return issuer.authorize(req) } catch (e: IssuerTimeoutException) { try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt) } catch (ie: InterruptedException) { log.warn("interrupted during back-off", ie) // and loop again } } attempt++ } }

steps.say: The inner catch logs and loops. sleep cleared the flag before throwing, so nothing remembers the request, and the loop has no limit. If the issuer is down during a rollout, this thread retries until the pod is killed. Before reading on, decide what the method should do when it is interrupted.
Restore the flag first, then stop retrying and tell the caller why. Wrapping the cause in your own exception is fine, as long as the flag is set before you throw. Add a retry limit while you're here.
steps.code: AuthResult authorize(AuthRequest req) { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return issuer.authorize(req); } catch (IssuerTimeoutException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; // 1. bounded retries try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // 2. restore the request throw new AuthCancelledException(req.id(), ie); // 3. stop, and say why } } } }

alt.html: fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): AuthResult { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return issuer.authorize(req) } catch (e: IssuerTimeoutException) { if (attempt == 3) throw e // 1. bounded retries try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt) } catch (ie: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // 2. restore the request throw AuthCancelledException(req.id, ie) // 3. stop, and say why } } attempt++ } }

steps.say: Now the caller, say an executor shutting down, sees the interrupt flag still set on its worker thread, and the payment is reported as cancelled instead of being retried forever. If authorize could simply declare throws InterruptedException, that would be even simpler: then there is nothing to restore.

lab.title: Make the outbox relay stop on interrupt
steps: Run the tests. All five fail, and the run is slow, because each test waits 5 seconds for a relay that never stops.
Read OutboxRelay.run(). Find the two ways it ignores an interrupt: while sleeping, and while busy with full batches.
Change the loop condition so it checks Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() once per batch. Finish the batch in hand before checking.
Handle the InterruptedException from sleep by restoring the flag and leaving the loop.
Run the tests until all five pass, then run them once more.
hints: Put the try around the whole while loop. Then the catch block runs once, restores the flag, and run() returns.
If the loop ends because isInterrupted() returned true, the flag is still set. You only need to restore it after an InterruptedException.
The "finishes the batch" test counts messages: the total must be a multiple of the batch size. Don't check the flag inside the for loop over the batch.

drill.title: Write an interruptible poller from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a Runnable that polls a Supplier<List<String>> and prints each item. When the list is empty it sleeps 100 ms. It must stop when interrupted, while sleeping or while busy, and leave the flag set when it returns. Then compare.

answer.html: Runnable poller = () -> { try { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { List<String> batch = source.get(); batch.forEach(System.out::println); if (batch.isEmpty()) Thread.sleep(100); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // sleep cleared it; put it back } };

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: val poller = Runnable { try { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) { val batch = source.get() batch.forEach(::println) if (batch.isEmpty()) Thread.sleep(100) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // sleep cleared it; put it back } }

recap: A thread is NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING or TERMINATED. RUNNABLE includes waiting for a core and sitting in native I/O.
BLOCKED means waiting for a synchronized monitor. Threads parked on explicit locks show WAITING.
join() waits for a thread to end and makes everything it wrote visible to you. sleep() does neither.
interrupt() only sets a flag. Blocking calls like sleep, wait, join and take throw InterruptedException and clear the flag first.
When you catch InterruptedException, rethrow it or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). Never just log it.
Daemon threads don't keep the JVM alive and can die mid-work. Thread.stop() is gone (removed in JDK 26), so cancellation is always cooperative.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "Why can't I just catch InterruptedException and log it? The thread keeps working, so what's the harm?" Answer them in your own words.
explain.answer: Interrupt is how the rest of the system asks your thread to stop: executors, shutdown hooks and frameworks all use it. When sleep or wait throws InterruptedException, it clears the interrupt flag first. If you only log, the request is gone and nobody above you can tell it was ever made, so the loop keeps running and shutdown hangs until the process is killed. Either let the exception propagate, or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to put the flag back and then stop what you're doing.

deeper.html:
Not every blocking call listens to interrupts.

sleep, wait, join, BlockingQueue.take and Lock.lockInterruptibly throw InterruptedException. A thread blocked on an NIO InterruptibleChannel is different: the Javadoc says the channel is closed, the flag is set and the thread gets a ClosedByInterruptException. So interrupting a thread that is writing to a FileChannel closes the file for everyone who shares that channel.

Plain synchronized does not respond at all. A thread that is BLOCKED waiting for a monitor stays blocked when you interrupt it; only the flag changes. A platform thread reading a classic java.net.Socket stream may also sit there until data arrives. For those, set a timeout (a socket read timeout, tryLock with a timeout) so the thread wakes up regularly and can check its flag.

Two smaller facts. Interrupts are part of the memory model too: if T1 interrupts T2, everything T1 did before the interrupt is visible to T2 once T2 sees the interrupt (by catching the exception or reading the flag). And JDK 27's Javadoc for interrupt() notes that interrupting a thread that is not alive still records the request in the reference implementation, so do not count on an interrupt before start() being dropped.
